title: Why Bees Matter
paras: Bees are small, but their work is enormous. When a bee visits a flower to drink nectar, grains of pollen stick to its body. At the next flower, some of this pollen falls off. This process is called pollination, and many plants need it to produce fruit and seeds. Without it, a flower can finish its life without making anything new.

Much of the food on our tables depends on this simple service. Apples, almonds, tomatoes, pumpkins and many other crops grow better when bees visit them. Farmers know this very well. Some of them even rent boxes of bees and place them in their fields during the flowering season. Scientists say that a large part of the world's food crops benefit from animal pollinators, and bees are the most important group.

Unfortunately, bees are in danger in many places. Farmers sometimes spray strong chemicals to kill insects that damage crops, and these chemicals can also harm bees. Cities and large farms have replaced meadows full of wild flowers with concrete and a single kind of plant, so bees find less food. Changes in the climate can also confuse them, because flowers may open earlier or later than usual.

The good news is that ordinary people can help. You can plant flowers on a balcony or in a garden, choosing different kinds that bloom in different months. You can leave a small corner of grass uncut and avoid chemical sprays. Another idea is to buy honey from local beekeepers, who look after their bees with care. If a bee lands on you, stay calm, because it only stings when it feels threatened. Protecting bees means protecting our own food. Even a small garden can become a safe home for many bees.

qs.q: What is pollination?
o: Pollen moving from one flower to another

title: The Deep Ocean
paras: The ocean covers more than two thirds of our planet, yet we know less about its deepest parts than about the surface of the Moon. The deep ocean begins about two hundred metres under the water, where sunlight slowly disappears. Below one thousand metres, there is no light at all. It is a world of darkness, great pressure and very cold water.

The pressure in the deep sea is so strong that it would crush a human body. To visit these places, scientists use special submarines with thick walls, or robots controlled from a ship. These machines carry lights and cameras, and they often bring back surprising pictures. Each journey shows new animals that nobody has seen before.

Animals in the deep have found clever ways to live without sunlight. Some fish make their own light, which is called bioluminescence. They use it to attract food, to find a partner or to scare enemies. Others have huge mouths and sharp teeth, because food is rare and they must catch whatever passes by. Many creatures are soft, slow and pale, and they save energy by moving as little as possible.

The deep ocean is also important for people. It stores a large amount of carbon and helps to control the climate. Unfortunately, it is under threat. Rubbish sinks to the bottom, and some companies want to dig the seabed for metals. Because deep animals grow slowly, damaged areas may need hundreds of years to recover. Many scientists therefore ask governments to protect the deep sea before it is too late. Every new discovery reminds us how much there still is to learn. Although the journey is difficult, it is one of the most exciting areas of science today.

qs.q: Where does the deep ocean begin?
o: About two hundred metres under the water

title: A Night at the Museum
paras: When the visitors go home and the lights go down, a museum does not go to sleep. At night, a small team of workers walks quietly through the halls. They check the rooms, look at the thermometers and make sure that nothing has changed. Their job is to protect objects that may be hundreds or even thousands of years old.

Old objects are very delicate, and their worst enemies are light, heat and damp air. Strong light slowly changes the colour of paper, cloth and paintings. Heat can make wood crack, and too much moisture helps mould to grow. For this reason, many rooms are kept dim, and the temperature and humidity stay almost the same all day and all night. Machines measure them every minute and send a warning if the numbers change.

Some objects are kept in special glass cases with their own air. A very old book, for example, may lie open on a soft support so that its pages are not bent. Staff are not allowed to touch most items with bare hands, because the natural oils on the skin can leave marks. They wear thin gloves and carry objects with great care. Insects such as moths can also eat cloth and paper, so the museum checks traps every week.

Another important job is repair work, which is called conservation. A conservator cleans a statue gently, fills a small crack or removes old glue. The aim is not to make the object look new, but to stop it from becoming worse. Every action is written in a report, so that future experts know what was done. Thanks to this patient work, children today can look at the same objects that people admired long ago, and so can their grandchildren.

qs.q: What do night workers do in a museum?
o: They check the rooms and protect the objects.

title: Healthy Habits for Students
paras: Student life is busy. There are lectures, homework, exams and often a part-time job. Many students think that they have no time to look after their health, but small daily habits can make a big difference. A healthy body helps the brain to learn, to remember and to stay calm during difficult weeks.

The first habit is sleep. Most young adults need between seven and nine hours every night. During sleep, the brain organises what you studied during the day. Students who stay awake all night before an exam often forget more than they learn. It is better to finish studying early and go to bed at a regular time. Switching off the phone an hour before bed also helps you to fall asleep.

The second habit is eating well. Breakfast gives energy for the morning, and fruit, vegetables, eggs and whole grains are good choices. Sugary drinks and fast food may give quick energy, but you soon feel tired again. Drinking enough water is just as important, because even a little dryness in the body can make it hard to concentrate.

Finally, move your body and rest your mind. A thirty-minute walk, a short game of football or a few exercises in your room reduce stress and improve your mood. When you study, take a five-minute break every hour and look away from the screen. Talk to friends and family when you feel under pressure, because sharing a problem makes it lighter. You do not need to change everything at once. Choose one habit this week, and add another next week. These habits cost little money, and they will help you to feel stronger and more confident during the whole year, not only before exams.
